title: Portfolio, Interview Prep, and Career Launch
summary: Skills get you interviews only if people can see them. Today you polish your GitHub, write a targeted resume, and rehearse common GenAI interview questions covering transformers, RAG, fine-tuning, and system design. You also set up habits to keep lea
content:
# Portfolio, Interview Prep, and Career Launch ##### "Tell me about a time your model was wrong" A candidate in Bengaluru was interviewing for a GenAI engineer role. The technical screen had gone well — he explained attention correctly, described RAG cleanly, knew the difference between LoRA and full fine-tuning. Then the interviewer asked: *"Tell me about a time your model gave a wrong answer. What did you do?"* He said his projects had worked well and he had not hit major issues. He did not get the offer. The interviewer's feedback, relayed through the recruiter, was blunt: *"He's read about GenAI. I'm not convinced he's shipped it. Everyone who has shipped has a hallucination story."* Another candidate the same week answered: *"My scholarship bot cited 'Clause 7.4' for a rule that was actually in 5.2. I found it through the trace — retrieval was correct, generation invented the clause number. I added a check that every number in the answer must appear in the retrieved context. It caught four more cases in the eval set."* She got the offer. **Debugging stories are the strongest signal you can give.** They prove you have built something real, because only people who ship encounter these problems. Today is about making your work visible and being able to talk about it. ##### GitHub as your primary credential For engineering roles, your GitHub is read before your resume. Make it readable in ninety seconds. **Your profile:** - **Profile README** — a repository named after your username. Three sentences on what you build, then links to your two or three best projects with one-line descriptions. - **Pin 3–6 repositories.** Quality over quantity, and pin them in order of impressiveness. - **Delete or archive tutorial repos.** `titanic-classification`, `todo-app`, and `learning-python` actively hurt. Someone scanning your profile should see only work you would defend. - **Bio and location.** Recruiters filter by both. **Each pinned repo needs**, from Day 44: - A README leading with the problem and a live link - A screenshot or GIF - Real numbers - A limitations section - Working setup instructions **A useful test:** open your profile in an incognito window and give yourself sixty seconds. Can you tell what this person builds and how good they are? If not, neither can a hiring manager. ##### The resume One page. Two if you have five-plus years of experience, which as a beginner you do not. **Structure:** ``` NAME | City | email | github.com/user | linkedin.com/in/user | portfolio.dev SUMMARY (2 lines, optional) GenAI engineer building RAG and agent systems. Shipped a multilingual scholarship assistant serving 340+ users with 89% benchmark accuracy. PROJECTS ← FIRST if you have no relevant work experience [Project name] | tech stack | [live link] [repo] • Built X that does Y for Z users, achieving [number] • Improved [metric] from A to B by [specific technique] • Deployed as [architecture], costing ₹N per query EXPERIENCE / INTERNSHIPS SKILLS EDUCATION ``` **Projects go above experience if your experience is unrelated.** A recruiter reading a GenAI resume wants to see GenAI work in the first third of the page. **Bullets must contain numbers.** Compare: - ❌ "Built a chatbot using LangChain and OpenAI" - ✅ "Built a multilingual RAG assistant over a 62-page government PDF; improved retrieval hit-rate from 55% to 89% via hybrid search and cross-encoder reranking; 340 users in month one" The second says what you built, for whom, what you measured, and what you did to improve it. **Skills section — group and be honest:** ``` Languages Python, SQL, JavaScript (basic) GenAI RAG, prompt engineering, LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning, agents, embeddings, evaluation (RAGAS, LLM-as-judge) Frameworks PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, LangChain, FastAPI Infra Docker, Chroma, pgvector, AWS (S3, EC2), GitHub Actions ``` Do not list something you cannot discuss for two minutes. Everything on the resume is fair game, and being caught padding is fatal. **Tailor per application.** Read the job description, mirror its vocabulary where it is honest to do so, and reorder your projects so the most relevant is first. Twenty tailored applications beat two hundred generic ones. ##### The interview loop Typical process for a GenAI role in India: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Recruiter screen
15-20 min"] --> B["Technical screen
45-60 min"] B --> C["Take-home or
live coding"] C --> D["System design
45-60 min"] D --> E["Behavioural /
team fit"] E --> F["Offer"] ``` Each stage tests something different, and preparing for the wrong one is a common mistake. ##### Conceptual questions Twenty questions worth writing out in full. Your assignment is to answer all of them in writing — the writing is what surfaces the gaps. **Fundamentals** 1. What is self-attention, and why does it beat RNNs for long sequences? 2. Why divide by √d_k in scaled dot-product attention? 3. What is multi-head attention buying you over single-head? 4. How does positional encoding work, and why is it necessary? 5. What is the difference between encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder architectures? **Training and adaptation** 6. Walk through pretraining → SFT → RLHF. What does each stage add? 7. When would you fine-tune instead of using RAG? 8. Explain LoRA. Why is the B matrix initialised to zeros? 9. What is QLoRA, and what does it cost you? 10. What is catastrophic forgetting and how do you avoid it? **RAG** 11. Walk through a RAG pipeline end to end. 12. How do you choose a chunk size? 13. Why hybrid search instead of pure vector search? 14. What does a reranker do, and where does it sit? 15. Your RAG system gives a wrong answer. How do you debug it? **Production** 16. How do you evaluate an LLM application? 17. How do you defend against prompt injection? 18. How would you cut the cost of an LLM feature by 50%? 19. What do you monitor in a production LLM system? 20. What is the difference between temperature and top-p? **Answer structure that works:** definition in one sentence, mechanism in two or three, a concrete example from your own project, and a trade-off or limitation. Roughly ninety seconds. That last element — naming the trade-off — is what distinguishes someone who understands from someone who memorised. For question 15, use the diagnostic table from Day 35: check the trace, determine whether the correct chunk was retrieved, and the answer to that determines whether you fix retrieval or generation. Interviewers love this question precisely because it separates the two groups. ##### System design The stage most candidates under-prepare, and the one that most determines seniority. **A typical prompt:** *"Design a customer support assistant for an e-commerce company with 2 million users and 50,000 support articles."* **A structure that works:** ``` 1. CLARIFY (3-5 min) — do not skip this - What languages? Query volume? Latency budget? - Should it take actions (issue refunds) or only answer? - What is the escalation path to a human? - Data residency constraints? 2. HIGH-LEVEL DESIGN (10 min) [Draw: ingestion pipeline | retrieval | generation | guardrails | monitoring] 3. DEEP DIVE (15-20 min) — follow the interviewer's interest - Chunking strategy and why - Hybrid retrieval + reranking - Prompt design with grounding and refusal - Guardrails: injection, moderation, PII 4. SCALE AND COST (10 min) - 2M users × 0.5 queries/day = 1M queries/day - Model routing: 80% to a small model - Caching: ~30% hit rate on FAQ-shaped queries - Estimated ₹X/day; here is how I would halve it 5. FAILURE MODES (5 min) - LLM API down → cached responses + graceful degradation - Retrieval returns nothing → refuse and escalate - Hallucination → grounding checks + citations + feedback loop ``` **Three things that impress in this format.** Asking clarifying questions before drawing anything. Quantifying — actual QPS, actual cost estimates, actual latency budget. And volunteering failure modes before being asked. Practise by designing three systems out loud, with a timer: a support assistant, a document processing pipeline, and a code review agent. ##### The behavioural round Prepare four stories in STAR form (Situation, Task, Action, Result). The ones that come up: - **A technical problem you debugged.** Have the hallucination story ready. - **Something you got wrong** and what you changed. - **A trade-off you made** and why. - **Something you learned quickly** under pressure. **The hallucination story is close to mandatory for GenAI roles.** Structure it as: what the system said, how you found out, what the root cause was, what you changed, and how you verified the fix. Ninety seconds. And prepare questions to ask them. "How do you evaluate your LLM features?" and "What does your monitoring stack look like?" signal that you think about production. "What's the biggest reliability problem you're facing?" often produces a genuinely interesting conversation. ##### Staying current The field moves fast, but less fast than the noise suggests. Fundamentals from Days 21–24 have been stable since 2017. **A sustainable weekly rhythm — about three hours:** - **One paper**, skimmed properly: abstract, figures, conclusion, then decide whether to read fully. Use Papers with Code or the Hugging Face daily papers. - **One thing built.** Even small. Reading about a technique is not knowing it. - **Follow a few practitioners** rather than the whole timeline. Signal over volume. **Sources worth the time:** Hugging Face blog and daily papers, Simon Willison's blog (excellent practical LLM coverage), Sebastian Raschka's newsletter, Lilian Weng's deep dives, and `mlabonne/llm-course` on GitHub. **Ignore:** most Twitter/LinkedIn hype, "prompt engineering secrets" content, and anything promising that a technique from last month is now obsolete. ##### Community and networking Referrals convert several times better than cold applications. That is not about knowing people already — it is about being visible. **What works, in rough order of return:** - **Write about what you built.** A blog post explaining one hard decision from your capstone doubles as a portfolio piece and interview rehearsal. Two or three good posts beat twenty shallow ones. - **Attend local meetups.** PyData and AI meetups run in Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad, Delhi NCR, and Chennai. Going three times and talking to people is worth more than a hundred LinkedIn connections. - **Contribute to open source.** Start with documentation fixes in libraries you use — LangChain, Transformers, Chroma. A merged PR is a verifiable credential. - **Publish something small.** A LoRA adapter or a dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, with a proper model card. - **Answer questions** in Discord and forums for tools you know. Visible competence compounds. **Realistic expectations for the Indian market:** GenAI engineer roles concentrate in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, NCR, and Chennai, with growing remote options. Entry-level and product-startup roles weigh portfolio heavily; larger enterprises still weigh DSA rounds, so keep some LeetCode practice if you are targeting them. Expect the process to take one to three months of consistent effort — and applications to convert at a low single-digit percentage even when you are good, which is normal and not a signal about you. ##### Common mistakes - **Tutorial repos left visible**, diluting your good work. - **A README with no live link and no numbers.** - **A resume listing technologies instead of outcomes.** - **Skills you cannot discuss for two minutes.** - **Mass-applying** instead of tailoring twenty applications. - **No debugging story** — the interview-losing gap. - **Skipping clarifying questions** in system design and drawing immediately. - **No cost estimates** in a system design round. - **Claiming projects worked perfectly.** Nobody believes it. - **Chasing every new model release** instead of deepening fundamentals. - **Only applying online** and never building visibility. - **Giving up after thirty applications.** The conversion rate is genuinely low. ##### Hands-on: make it visible Your practical task polishes your GitHub and drafts a GenAI resume. Do the incognito sixty-second test on your profile first, then fix what fails it. For the resume, rewrite every project bullet to contain a number — if you cannot find one, go measure something. That constraint alone will improve the document more than any formatting change. The mini project is a portfolio site showcasing your capstone. Keep it simple: GitHub Pages with a clean single page is entirely sufficient, and a beautiful site with weak projects fools nobody. For each project, show a screenshot, a one-line description, the key result, and links to the live demo and repo. Above the fold, someone should see what you build and how well. The assignment answers twenty interview questions in writing plus one mock system design. **Write them out fully rather than thinking them through** — writing exposes the questions you thought you understood. Then record yourself answering five of them out loud and listen back; you will hear the ones where you ramble. For the system design, use the five-step structure with a timer, and speak it aloud rather than just sketching, because the interview is verbal. ##### Key takeaways - **Your GitHub is read before your resume.** Pin three to six strong projects, delete the tutorials, and make each README lead with the problem, a live link, and real numbers. - **Every resume bullet needs a number** — what you built, for whom, and what measurably improved. - **Have a debugging story ready.** "My model was wrong, here's how I found it and fixed it" is the strongest evidence that you have actually shipped something. - **System design rewards clarifying questions, quantified estimates, and volunteered failure modes** — practise it out loud with a timer. - **Depth beats novelty-chasing.** Three hours a week of one paper and one thing built, plus local community visibility, compounds faster than following every model release.
